title: What a Fire Needs
logline: On a hill-country ridge where coarse grassland has burned in the dry months for as long as anyone has recorded it, three blocks of the same slope stand side by side: a fire trace slashed to bare soil every year and green again within weeks, a closed canopy under which the grass simply is not there while the canopy stands, and a block where the planted trees that held the ground were taken out root plate and all, so that nothing of them comes up at all.
human_question: What is the difference between holding something down, crowding it out, and taking away the ground it grew from?

place.what_kind_of_place: A range of low mountains immediately south-west of a hill-country town, rising from about six hundred metres to about twelve hundred, declared an environmental protection area and holding a conservation forest, a set of communication masts on the highest ground, and the upper edge of a university's land on its lower slopes. The top of the range is coarse tussock grassland of the kind that covers a great deal of the island's central highlands: knee-high bunch grass, bare reddish soil showing between the tufts, scattered rock, and small tongues of natural forest pushed into the folds and gullies where fire cannot easily run. Below that, on ground that was bare and eroding fifty years ago, blocks of an exotic pine were planted as a nurse crop in straight rows; under those rows, over the following decades, broad-leaved native and naturalised trees were put in under measured amounts of light, and in one block the pines themselves were finally taken out, leaving a young mixed woodland standing where a plantation stood. The working equipment is a bush knife, a mammoty, a crowbar, a planting bar, a tape, numbered aluminium tags on stems, and a plot register. There is nothing mechanised anywhere on the slope.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the concept is laid out on the ground in three adjacent blocks, and from height the three read as three different colours. Wide, at either end of the day, the whole range separates into a straw-coloured top, a dark closed canopy below it, and between them a hard line that runs along the hill for kilometres and moves a few metres a decade. That is the most beautiful thing the place produces and it is also the whole film: on one side of the line the grass is cut back every year and comes straight back, on the other side it is not there at all. Close, the place is very small evidence: ash against a green edge three weeks after slashing, a grass runner crossing bare soil, leaf litter under closed shade with no grass in it, a pit where a stump and its root plate were levered out and the soil put back, a numbered tag on a stem planted in a particular year, and the register that says which block is which. And the slope has one thing that can be filmed only by waiting: fire comes up these hills in the dry months, and along one stretch of the line it has not come for years, because what it needs is not there.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Three speeds at once, and the film is the difference between them. Fastest: the slashed trace. It is cut back to soil and within a few weeks of rain the tussocks are back, because the roots and the seed were never removed, so the same work has to be done again next year and the year after. Slower: the canopy. Where the crowns have closed, grass does not come up, and nothing about that is permanent either, since it holds only as long as the shade holds and a gap opens it again. Slowest and the only one that does not reverse: the block where the planted trees were levered out with the root plate, where the ground was closed behind them and where, years later, no seedling of that tree comes up anywhere, because the thing that produced them is not on the slope any more. Against all three, the dry season comes round on its own schedule, and the boundary between grass and closed forest creeps in one direction by a few metres a decade.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry months, when the grass goes straw-coloured and stands out against the canopy from any distance, and when fire is a real possibility on the slope rather than a subject for conversation. The ridge wants the first hour and the last hour, when low sun rakes across the tussocks and every tongue of forest in a gully throws its own shadow; it wants mist mornings, when the canopy blocks appear and disappear as cloud moves through them; and it is worth filming at noon for the opposite reason, when the three blocks flatten into one colour and the line vanishes. The close work follows the conservation calendar rather than the light: traces are cut before the dry weeks, planting is done at the start of the rains, and a stump comes out when somebody has decided to take it out.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about one hillside and three ways of getting rid of a plant. A ridge of straw-coloured grass at first light with dark forest below it; a bush knife taken through tussocks along a trace, and the same trace green again a few weeks later; ash and a burnt edge; leaf litter under closed shade with no grass in it; the exact line where light returns and the grass resumes within a metre; a stump and its root plate levered out with a crowbar and the pit filled; numbered tags on young stems; a plot register in a folder; cloud coming through a young mixed woodland that was a plantation of one species ten years ago. With nothing said over it, anyone who likes open hill country, or patient ground-level work, or the plain question of why a plant keeps coming back in one place and never appears in another, has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same slope becomes the sources' distinction between three kinds of abandoning, which is otherwise a list of three technical words. The texts separate pressing something down so that it is held for a while, displacing it with the factor that opposes it for as long as that lasts, and cutting it off so that it does not arise again, and they say only the last one is what their path does. They also say a thing needs a ground in order to arise and to continue at all. A hillside where those three are being done to the same plant in three adjacent blocks carries the distinction without anybody having to recite it, and the film's one unscheduled event, a dry-season fire that does not come where its fuel is gone, carries the argument about ground. The voice never says the grass is a defilement and never says the hillside is a person. It says the sources make a three-way distinction that ordinary language collapses into one word, that they insist nothing a camera can see tells you which of the three you are looking at in a person, and that a slope is a place where, for a plant, you can actually tell.

sequence.on_screen: First light, high and along the range. A straw-coloured top of tussock grass, a dark closed canopy below it, and a hard line between them running along the hill out of frame. Low sun across the tufts. Nothing moving but cloud.
sequence.voice: Something used to come up this slope every dry season. Along one stretch of that line it still does, and along another stretch it has not for years. Everything in this film is the difference between three ways of making something stop.

sequence.on_screen: The trace. A strip cut down to bare reddish soil along the ridge, the cut tussocks lying where they fell. Then the same strip in the same frame some weeks later, green at the edges and closing over. Ash on one side of it.
sequence.voice: The old analysis says abandoning is three things and not one [C098-P4:L205]. The first is pressing down. It is what an ordinary settled mind does to what opposes it, and the sources are exact that what has been pressed down was there before and is there afterwards [C098-P4:L209]. This work is done once a year, every year, because nothing under it has been removed.

sequence.on_screen: Under a closed canopy. Leaf litter, bare stems, seedlings of other things, and no grass at all. Then a slow move to the edge, where light comes back in and the tussocks resume within a metre, as if drawn.
sequence.voice: The second kind is abandoning by the factor that opposes it, which the sources place in the long preparatory work rather than at the end [C098-P4:L211]. It is real and it is not permanent. Nothing here was taken out. The grass is absent because something else is standing over it, and it is absent for exactly as long as that lasts.

sequence.on_screen: A pit on the lower slope: a stump and its whole root plate levered out with a crowbar, the hole open, the soil going back. Around it a young mixed woodland with numbered tags on the stems. No seedling of the removed tree anywhere in frame.
sequence.voice: The third kind is cutting off, so that the thing does not run on again [C098-P4:L247], and the sources give their own picture for it. A young tree cut at the root before it has fruited: the fruit that never formed does not appear, does not form and does not come [C098-P4:L145]. That is their image, not ours. What was planted here to hold this ground is out, and nothing of it comes up.

sequence.on_screen: The ground itself at arm's length. A hand's width of soil in section: root mat, seed, a runner crossing bare grit. Then the burnt edge again, and the unburnt side where litter lies deep under shade.
sequence.voice: Underneath all three the sources put one condition. For a thing to arise and to keep going there has to be a ground for it, and they name what that ground is [C098-P4:L149]. And they are careful about what is removed: not what is already over, and not what has not happened [C098-P4:L143]. What a fire needs on this hill is fuel, and along one stretch of that line the fuel is not there.

sequence.on_screen: Rain arriving across the range. The trace darkening and the cut tussocks flattening; the canopy blocks taking it silently. Then the same three blocks from height in flat mid-morning light, when the line between them almost disappears.
sequence.voice: The other book puts it in one sentence. Ordinary good practice can push a tendency aside or hold it down and it can come back; what it describes is a change after which the thing does not return, because the ground it grew from has been taken away [C016-P:L76–L82]. It also says, twice over, that there is no shorter road than the graded work taken in order [C016-P:L62].

sequence.on_screen: Last light along the ridge. The masts on the high ground, the grassland going orange, the canopy going black. A folder of plot records closed on a knee. The line still there, invisible in ten minutes.
sequence.voice: Three things this film is not saying. The sources define each of their stages by what has been given up, not by rank or accomplishment, and nothing a camera can see verifies any of it in any person [C098-M:L11–L27]. What they describe as the cutting moment has a single object and does four things at once, and it is not an experience anyone could report [C016-P:L54]. And a hillside is a hillside. People burn these slopes for fodder and for hunting, as people have for centuries, and nothing here is a judgement on them.

concept_merge.why_together: C098 supplies the distinction and C016 supplies the sentence that keeps it from hardening. C098's Pradeepika section states that abandoning is threefold, pressing down, abandoning by the opposing factor, and cutting off [C098-P4:L205], defines the first as what mundane concentration does to what opposes it, with the hindrances present before and after [C098-P4:L209], places the second in the preparatory purifications [C098-P4:L211], and defines the third as abandoning by the noble path so that the thing does not run on again [C098-P4:L247]. It gives its own image for the third, a young tree cut at the root before fruiting, whose fruit does not appear, does not form and does not come [C098-P4:L145]. It adds the condition the film's one unscheduled event depends on: for a thing to arise and continue there must be a ground for it [C098-P4:L149]; and it is careful that what is removed is neither the past nor the future [C098-P4:L143]. C016 states the same separation in a single clause, holding down or pushing aside against a change after which the thing does not return because its ground is gone [C016-P:L76–L82], insists there is no shorter road than graded work in order [C016-P:L62], and rules out reading the decisive moment as an epiphany, since it has one object and performs four functions at once [C016-P:L54]. A hillside on which three different methods are being used against the same plant in three adjacent blocks puts the distinction on the ground, where it can be tested by looking, and the fire that no longer arrives puts the argument about ground on the ground with it.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That ordinary language has one word for three completely different situations, and that only pressure and time tell them apart. Said flat, the three kinds of abandoning are three technical terms with no felt difference between them. Put on a slope, they become three pieces of work with three different futures: one that must be repeated every single year, one that holds only while something else stands over it, and one that has no future at all because the thing that produced it is gone. The film also gets the concept's hardest clause for free, because a fire is the clearest case of a thing that cannot arise without a ground, and a slope where the fuel has been removed is not a slope where the fire is being fought. This idea has been rewritten off its previous subject entirely. Its earlier version filmed an identifiable shopkeeper years after leaving a trade the whole neighbourhood remembers, and asked that person on camera whether the old pull was gone or only managed. That is dropped: it puts a real person's past occupation on screen as something to be left behind, it re-tells a history the person may have spent years letting fade, and it invites the viewer to read a stranger's steadiness as an attainment, which is the one thing this group must never do. The concepts are unchanged. The subject is now a place, with no person's history in it at all.

concept_links.why: The film is the digest's three kinds of abandoning and the condition underneath them, and nothing else from the concept. The threefold statement is spoken once [C098-P4:L205]; pressing down is spoken over an annually re-cut trace that is green again within weeks, which is the digest's own account of a thing that was there before and is there afterwards [C098-P4:L209]; abandoning by the opposing factor is spoken under a closed canopy at the exact metre where light returns and the grass resumes, which is what that kind is, real and not permanent [C098-P4:L211]; cutting off is spoken over a root plate levered out of the ground [C098-P4:L247], together with the source's own young-tree image, named on screen as the source's picture and not the film's [C098-P4:L145]; the requirement of a ground for arising and continuing is spoken over soil in section and over a burnt edge [C098-P4:L149]; and the care about past and future is spoken in the same beat [C098-P4:L143]. Every limit in the digest that bears on this film is honoured and one of them closes it. The stages are never presented as a status ladder or a ranking of people, and the closing beat states out loud that each stage is defined by what has been given up rather than by accomplishment and that nothing visible verifies it in anybody [C098-M:L11–L27]. No real person is labelled a noble person, framed as one, or implied to be one; there is no interview in the film and no person's history in it. The personal-growth reading is refused by construction, since the subject is a plant on a slope and the film's own limit beat says so. The source's two illustrations of defilements resurfacing, which the digest flags as teaching examples rather than facts about real people, are not cited, narrated or alluded to. The prosperity and worthy-of-gifts material is unused. Nobody's poverty, hardship or bad year appears anywhere, and the people who burn these slopes are named once, without blame, so that the film cannot be heard as saying their work is the defilement.

Two of this concept's statements are narrated and both are load-bearing. The separation of holding down and pushing aside from a change after which the thing does not return, because the ground it grew from is gone, is spoken over rain arriving on all three blocks at once, which is the moment the footage can hold a sentence about all three [C016-P:L76–L82]; and the insistence that there is no shorter road than the graded practice taken in order is spoken in the same beat, because a slope on which one block took thirty years is the honest place for it [C016-P:L62]. The closing beat carries the digest's sharpest correction, that the decisive moment has a single object and performs four set functions at once and is therefore not a breakthrough, a conversion or an emotional peak [C016-P:L54]. Every limit in the digest is honoured. The stages are not treated as labels for observable people and the film says so out loud. 'Everyone can be enlightened right now' is refused by the no-short-cut beat. The order of what goes first and last is not reproduced or mapped onto anything on the slope. The rebirth pathways, the counts, the treasure-house story and the lamp simile are not used at all, and the gender-sensitive clause the digest flags for expert checking is not touched. Nothing on screen is offered as the unconditioned, and no still shot of the closed canopy is allowed to stand for it.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the texts separate three things ordinary speech calls by one name: pressing a tendency down, so that it is held for a while and returns; displacing it with the factor that opposes it, which holds only while that lasts; and cutting it off so that it does not arise again, because the ground it grew from is gone. The hillside is an analogy for the distinction and the film says so; no claim is made about any person's inner state, nobody is described as having reached anything, and nobody's use of this land is judged.
what_must_be_real: The conservation work's own calendar and its own order. No trace is cut, no stump is pulled, no planting is done and no block is opened because the film asked for it, and no fire is lit, encouraged, permitted to run or filmed in a way that makes it look like an event staged for a camera. If no fire happens in the filming window, the film has the slope without one. Nothing is cleared to improve a sight line and no tag, plot marker or boundary is moved. The people who work the slope are filmed as people doing work, are not named, are not followed, are not interviewed and are not asked to confirm any doctrine. Nobody who grazes, burns or hunts on this range is filmed in a way that identifies them, and no fire is attributed to anyone.
position_hint: early in the group, and before any film that turns on the difference between a change that holds and a change that does not: it is the plainest statement of the group's three-way distinction, it makes that distinction on ground rather than in a person, and it sets the group's ethical floor on its first outing by saying out loud that nothing visible verifies any of this in anybody. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting the three blocks read as a ladder of personal-growth levels, which is the digest's sharpest correction and the group's hardest floor.
Allowing any person on the slope to become an example of steadiness, patience or attainment. There is no interview in this film for exactly that reason.
Turning the grass into a vice and the canopy into a virtue, so that the film becomes an allegory and the hillside stops being a hillside.
Making the people who burn these grasslands into the film's antagonists, or implying that their fodder or hunting is the defilement the sources are talking about.
Sentimentalising the removed plantation into a redemption story about exotic species, or on the other side into a lament for a lost plantation. Neither is the film.
Filming or waiting for a fire in a way that encourages one, or that puts a crew, the forest or anybody's cattle in the way of one.
Letting a still shot of closed canopy in mist stand in for the unconditioned, which cannot be filmed.
Claiming more permanence for the cleared block than the ecology supports. It is a block where one species does not return, not a block where nothing will ever change.
Implying that the slope's condition is anybody's desert, or that the range's poorer soils are the result of anything anybody did.
drop_if: The three states cannot be found within sight of one another, so the film's whole comparison has to be assembled from separate hillsides.
The forest authority and the landholder will not allow the blocks, the trace and the plot records to be filmed on their own schedule.
The removal of stumps and root plates is historical only, with no comparable work anywhere on the range during the filming window, so the third kind would have to be staged.
The line between grassland and closed canopy does not read from height, which is the shot the whole film rests on.
Filming on the range cannot be done without identifying the people who graze or burn it.

connections.note: One film is about taking something apart so that it cannot come back, the other about putting separate things together so that they hold. They are the group's two ground-level films about what removal and composition actually look like.
Two films in which a fixed procedure, not a person, carries the concept, and in which the voice says out loud that nothing on screen is anybody's attainment.

selection.reason: Its three adjacent blocks are the concept itself, tested by looking rather than asserted, and the subject is a place with no person's history in it.

review.note: Rewritten into the footage-led shape on 2026-09-24, and the subject dropped entirely. The previous version filmed an identifiable shopkeeper years after giving up a trade the whole locality remembers, and asked that person on camera whether the old pull was gone or only managed. Three things were wrong with it and all three are fatal here: it puts a real person's past occupation on screen as a thing to be left behind, which the project's digests forbid doing with the sources' own livelihood examples; it re-tells a history the person may have spent years letting fade, in front of the neighbours who remember it; and it invites the viewer to read a stranger's composure as an attainment, which is the one reading this group must never permit. The concepts are unchanged and both links were re-tested from the digests. The subject is now a hill-country slope on which three kinds of removal are being done to the same plant in three adjacent blocks, with no interview, no named person and no person's history anywhere in it. The source's young-tree image is spoken once and named on screen as the source's picture. The requirement of a ground for arising is carried by a dry-season fire that does not come where its fuel is gone, which is the one thing in the film that cannot be scheduled. Every citation was checked line by line against C098's and C016's digest evidence and none was carried over from the old text. The closing beat states the digest's corrections about rank, about verification and about the decisive moment not being an experience, and adds a line that protects the people who burn these grasslands from becoming the film's antagonists.

suggested_location.name: The grassland ridge and the restoration blocks of the Hanthana range, above and south-west of Kandy

also_known_as.name: Hantana
also_known_as.meaning: the usual spelling of the range on maps and signboards; the highest of its seven peaks is recorded as Uura Kanda

also_known_as.name: patana
also_known_as.meaning: the coarse montane tussock grassland that covers the tops of ranges like this one; the wet patanas of the central highlands are maintained in that state largely by fire

also_known_as.name: nurse crop
also_known_as.meaning: a fast exotic species planted first on bare or eroded ground to create the shade and litter under which native trees can later be established, and removed once they are away

suggested_location.region: Kandy District, Central Province: the mountain range on the south-western side of the hill-country town, rising directly behind a university's land from about 600 to about 1,200 metres
suggested_location.why_here: Because the three kinds of removal exist here side by side on one hillside, in a place that is documented, institutional and able to consent. The range was declared an environmental protection area in 2010, it holds a conservation forest under the state forest authority, its top is patana grassland of the kind that exists in that state largely because it burns, and its lower slopes carry blocks of exotic pine planted decades ago on bare, eroding ground. Those blocks are the point. Published work describes a pine plantation on the lower part of this range used as a nurse crop for about thirty years: broad-leaved native and naturalised trees were transplanted under three different amounts of light in 2004, and the pines were taken out in 2010, leaving a young mixed woodland where a single-species plantation stood. So one slope holds a trace that is slashed and comes straight back, a canopy under which grass simply is not present, and a block from which the thing that held the ground was removed outright. The dry months add the one event the film cannot schedule, a grass fire that does not come where the fuel has gone. The district is well within reach of a crew, the bodies that would have to agree are a university and a forest department rather than a household, and there is no private grief, no livelihood arithmetic and nobody's history anywhere in the subject.
what_to_film: The range from height in the first and last half hour of the day, so the straw-coloured grassland, the closed canopy and the line between them separate into three bands, and again at noon when they flatten into one.
The line itself at ground level, walked slowly: the last tussock, the first closed shade, and the metre in between.
A fire trace immediately after cutting, and the same frame again some weeks later with the grass closing over it.
Under the closed canopy: litter, bare stems, seedlings of other species, and the complete absence of grass, held long enough to be believed.
A stump and root plate coming out with a crowbar, the open pit, and the soil going back, filmed as the work happens rather than arranged.
Numbered tags on planted stems and the plot register in a folder, close, without anybody's name legible.
Soil in section at arm's length: root mat, seed, grit, and a grass runner crossing bare ground.
Cloud and mist moving through the young mixed woodland, held still and long, because it is the most beautiful thing on the slope and it is also the second kind of abandoning.
A burnt edge after a dry-season fire, if one happens, filmed plainly and without emphasis, and never encouraged or arranged.
The masts on the high ground against last light, as the one reminder that this is a used, administered hillside and not a wilderness.
suggested_location.access: By road from the hill-country town and then on footpaths and hiking tracks; the upper range is a declared environmental protection area with a conservation forest, so filming needs the state forest authority's written permission, and the restoration blocks on the lower slopes sit on university land, which means a second permission from the institution that holds them. Walking the ridge is straightforward in dry weather and unpleasant in wet; the slopes are steep, the grass hides loose rock, and leeches are a real nuisance after rain. Flying over the range cannot be assumed: there are communication masts on the high ground, the town and its airspace lie immediately to the north-east, and clearance would have to be sought and may be refused, in which case the three-band shot has to be taken from the ridge itself and from the peaks. Anything to do with fire, including filming a burnt edge after the event, should be arranged through the forest authority rather than locally, and no crew should be on the range in a dry spell without agreeing a withdrawal route first.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry months, when the grass is straw-coloured, the three bands read from any distance and fire is a live possibility on the slope. Within a day, the first and last hour for the range, and mist mornings for the canopy blocks. The close work has to be taken on the conservation calendar rather than on the light: traces are cut before the dry weeks, planting is done at the beginning of the rains, and stump removal happens when somebody has decided to do it. A second short visit is worth planning for whichever weeks a fire actually happens, since that cannot be arranged and must not be.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, and unverified on the ground. From the sources above: the range lies south-west of the hill-country town, was declared an environmental protection area in February 2010, reaches about 1,200 metres across seven peaks, holds a conservation forest under the state forest authority and carries communication masts on its high ground, with a university's land adjoining it. Published Sri Lankan material describes exotic pine used as a partner in ecological restoration on the lower part of this range for about thirty years; a study of a Caribbean pine plantation there reports broad-leaved species transplanted under three light treatments in 2004 and all pine trees removed in 2010, and concludes that such plantations can be replaced by native and naturalised species. Separate ecological material on the island's montane grasslands states that dry patanas are deliberately burnt in the dry months for fresh fodder and for hunting and that their existence is itself a result of fire. Three things the film depends on are inferences about this particular range rather than confirmed facts: that a slashed fire trace, a closed canopy block and a block from which stumps and root plates were physically removed can be found within sight of one another; that stump or root-plate removal is current work here rather than something finished a decade ago; and that the grass-to-canopy boundary reads as strongly from height as it appears to from the ground. The coordinates are the published position of the range itself, not a survey of any block, and no plot, compartment, institution or person has been identified or approached. No permission has been sought from the forest authority, the university or anyone else. No photograph of the restoration blocks, the trace or any of this work was found on Wikimedia Commons; the one image is of the range.

unknowns: Whether a slashed trace, a closed canopy block and a block cleared of stumps and root plates can all be found within sight of one another on this range.
Whether removal of stumps and root plates is current work here, or whether the pine removal is finished and only its result remains.
Whether the forest authority and the university that hold the ground will allow filming on their own work calendar, indoors and out.
Whether a dry-season fire falls inside a filming window at all, and whether a burnt edge can be filmed afterwards without the crew becoming a factor in how fire on the range is discussed.
Whether height can be obtained over the range, given the masts and the town's airspace, or whether the three-band view has to be taken from the ridge.
Whether the people who graze, burn or hunt on the range can be kept out of frame, or at least unidentifiable, without the film pretending they are not there.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is proposed by Claude from desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
